## What it is

The phrase echoes "straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel." Debates about Bayesian statistics focus on the prior: is it subjective, is it justified, how sensitive are the results to it? Meanwhile the **likelihood**, the data model, is accepted with little scrutiny. Yet the likelihood typically encodes far stronger assumptions: normal errors, independence, linearity, a particular link function, no measurement error. Those assumptions often matter far more than the prior.

## Why it matters

Sensitivity analyses that vary the prior while keeping the likelihood fixed can give false reassurance: "our results are robust to the prior!" Meanwhile a single outlier or a heavy-tailed error distribution can change the conclusion entirely under a different but equally reasonable likelihood. Frequentist methods also rest on likelihoods, or equivalent assumptions, so the camel is swallowed on both sides of the debate.

## How it works

Take estimating a location parameter from data that contain a few outliers. Changing the prior on the location from $\mathrm{N}(0, 1)$ to $\mathrm{N}(0, 10)$ hardly moves the posterior when $n$ is moderate. Changing the likelihood from normal to Student-$t$ with 3 degrees of freedom can move it a lot, because the normal likelihood lets outliers pull the estimate while the $t$ likelihood down-weights them.

## Simulated example

Data come from a normal distribution centred at 1, with a few gross outliers added. Compute the posterior mean under two priors × two likelihoods (by grid approximation) and compare how much each choice matters.

```{ojs}
import {rng, range, dnorm, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof nOut = Inputs.range([0, 8], {value: 3, step: 1, label: "Number of outliers"})
viewof outSize = Inputs.range([2, 20], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "Outlier size"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 99, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
camel = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const y = [...r.normals(30, 1, 1), ...range(nOut).map(() => outSize + r.normal(0, 1))];
  const grid = range(801).map(i => -4 + i * 0.02);
  const logT3 = z => -2 * Math.log(1 + z * z / 3);
  const post = (priorSd, like) => {
    const lp = grid.map(m => Math.log(dnorm(m, 0, priorSd)) + y.reduce((s, v) => s + (like === "Normal" ? -0.5 * (v - m) ** 2 : logT3(v - m)), 0));
    const mx = Math.max(...lp), w = lp.map(v => Math.exp(v - mx)), tot = w.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
    return w.reduce((s, wi, i) => s + wi * grid[i], 0) / tot;
  };
  return ["Normal", "Student-t (3 df)"].flatMap(like => [1, 10].map(ps => ({like, prior: `Prior N(0, ${ps})`, mean: post(ps, like)})));
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 220,
  marginLeft: 120,
  fy: {label: null},
  x: {label: "Posterior mean of the location (truth = 1)", grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["#2166ac", "#d6604d"]},
  marks: [Plot.dot(camel, {fy: "like", y: "prior", x: "mean", fill: "prior", r: 7}), Plot.ruleX([1], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3"})]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const g = (l, p) => camel.find(d => d.like === l && d.prior === p).mean;
  const priorEffect = Math.abs(g("Normal", "Prior N(0, 1)") - g("Normal", "Prior N(0, 10)"));
  const likeEffect = Math.abs(g("Normal", "Prior N(0, 10)") - g("Student-t (3 df)", "Prior N(0, 10)"));
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`Changing the prior (sd 1 → 10) moves the posterior mean by **${fmt(priorEffect, 3)}** (the gnat). Changing the likelihood (normal → t) moves it by **${fmt(likeEffect, 3)}** (the camel). With ${nOut} outliers, the choice of data model matters far more than the prior.`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- The likelihood usually carries stronger assumptions than the prior.
- Do sensitivity analysis on the data model, not just the prior.
- Robust likelihoods, model checking and measurement models deserve as much scrutiny as priors.
:::
